stem: In MCP's interaction model, who decides when a prompt is used?

options.text: The user, who explicitly selects it, for example as a slash command
options.why: Correct: prompts are user-controlled.

options.text: The model, which picks prompts automatically from context
options.why: That describes tools, which are model-controlled.

options.text: The host application, which attaches prompts using its own heuristics
options.why: That is how resources work: they are application-driven.

options.text: The server, which pushes prompts into the conversation when it sees fit
options.why: Servers define prompt content, but they do not decide when a prompt is used.

explanation: Prompts are user-controlled: the server offers templates and the user chooses one, typically from a slash-command menu. The spec stresses that this is about who decides when the prompt is used, not who writes it; the content comes from the server.

stem: Match each MCP primitive with the control model the specification describes for it.

options.text: Model-controlled
options.why: The language model discovers and invokes it based on context.

options.text: Application-driven
options.why: The host application decides how and when to include it as context.

options.text: User-controlled
options.why: The user explicitly selects it.

options.text: Server-controlled
options.why: The server pushes it into the model's context on its own; no primitive works this way.

explanation: The three server primitives differ by who is in control: tools are model-controlled, resources (including those discovered through templates) are application-driven, and prompts are user-controlled. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can place a new capability in the right primitive.

stem: Which JSON-RPC method does a client send to fetch the contents of a resource by its URI? Type the method name.
explanation: Clients discover resources with `resources/list` (and parameterised ones with `resources/templates/list`) and fetch contents with `resources/read`, passing the `uri`. The result has a `contents` array plus `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` caching hints.

stem: How is each MCP resource uniquely identified?

options.text: By an integer ID assigned when the client lists resources
options.why: There are no numeric resource IDs; the URI is the identity.

options.text: By a URI, such as `file:///project/src/main.rs`
options.why: Correct: every resource has a unique URI, with an optional MIME type alongside it.

options.text: By its `name`, which must be unique across all servers
options.why: `name` is descriptive; the URI is the identifier, and nothing is unique across servers.

options.text: By its MIME type and size together
options.why: `mimeType` and `size` describe the content; they do not identify it.

explanation: Resources are identified by URIs that follow RFC 3986. Standard schemes include `https://`, `file://` and `git://`, and servers may define custom schemes. A resource entry also carries a `name` and optionally a `title`, `description`, `mimeType`, `size` and icons.

stem: The contents of an MCP resource are returned either as a `text` field or as a base64-encoded `blob` field.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: text resources use `text`, binary resources use `blob` with base64-encoded data, and each carries its `uri` and usually a `mimeType`.

options.text: False
options.why: Resource contents really are one of these two forms; there is no third raw-bytes field.

explanation: `resources/read` returns `contents`, an array of items each holding the `uri`, an optional `mimeType`, and either `text` or `blob` (base64). Binary data MUST be properly encoded.

stem: A client calls `resources/list`. Which field in the result tells it that more results are available?

options.text: `hasMore: true`
options.why: `hasMore` belongs to completion results, not to paginated list results.

options.text: An `offset` the client increments
options.why: Clients never compute positions; the server hands out opaque cursors.

options.text: A non-null `nextCursor`
options.why: Correct: the client passes it back as `cursor` to get the next page.

options.text: `page` and `totalPages`
options.why: MCP uses opaque cursors, not numbered pages.

explanation: List operations (`resources/list`, `resources/templates/list`, `prompts/list`, `tools/list`) use cursor pagination. The server includes `nextCursor` when more results exist, the client sends it back as `cursor`, and a missing `nextCursor` means the end. Page size is the server's choice.

stem: Which JSON-RPC method does a client send to retrieve a prompt's messages with its arguments filled in? Type the method name.
explanation: Clients discover prompts with `prompts/list` and retrieve one with `prompts/get`, passing `name` and an `arguments` object. The server returns an optional `description` and a `messages` array ready to add to the conversation.

stem: Which values are valid in the `audience` annotation of a resource or content block?

options.text: `"public"` and `"private"`
options.why: Those are the values of `cacheScope`, a caching hint on results.

options.text: `"model"`, `"application"` and `"user"`
options.why: These echo the control models of the primitives, not annotation values.

options.text: `"user"` and `"assistant"`
options.why: Correct: `audience` is an array of roles, for example `["user", "assistant"]`.

options.text: `"user"`, `"assistant"` and `"system"`
options.why: MCP roles are only `user` and `assistant`; there is no `system` role.

explanation: Annotations have three optional fields: `audience` (an array of `"user"` and/or `"assistant"`), `priority` (0.0 to 1.0, where 1 means effectively required) and `lastModified` (an ISO 8601 timestamp). Clients use them to filter, prioritise and sort context.

stem: Which of these capabilities is best exposed as a tool rather than a resource?

options.text: Creating a Jira ticket from the conversation
options.why: Correct: it has side effects and the model decides when to do it, so it is a tool.

options.text: A log file at a fixed URI that the user can pin to the chat
options.why: Fixed, addressable data selected by the user or app is a resource.

options.text: The project's README, which the host attaches as background context
options.why: Read-only context chosen by the application is the classic resource.

options.text: The database schema, so the model knows the table names
options.why: Static descriptive data the app can attach; a resource fits.

explanation: Ask two questions: does it act on the world, and who decides when it happens? Actions with side effects that the model chooses are tools. Read-only data identified by a URI and included at the application's discretion is a resource.

stem: Under 2026-07-28, how must a server answer `resources/read` for a URI that does not exist?

options.text: A JSON-RPC error with code `-32601` (Method not found)
options.why: The method exists; it is the parameter, the URI, that is wrong.

options.text: A result with an empty `contents` array
options.why: Servers MUST NOT do this: an empty array could also mean an existing but empty resource.

options.text: A JSON-RPC error with code `-32602` (Invalid params)
options.why: Correct: 2026-07-28 changed resource-not-found to `-32602` to align with JSON-RPC.

options.text: A JSON-RPC error with code `-32002`
options.why: That was the code in earlier revisions; clients SHOULD still accept it for backwards compatibility.

explanation: The 2026-07-28 revision moved resource-not-found from `-32002` to `-32602`, optionally with the URI in `error.data`. Servers SHOULD use `-32603` for internal errors and MUST NOT return an empty `contents` array for a missing resource. Clients SHOULD still accept `-32002` from older servers.

stem: What is the maximum number of suggestions a server may return in the `values` array of a single `completion/complete` response? Type a number.
explanation: Completion results hold at most 100 values, ranked by relevance, plus an optional `total` count and a `hasMore` flag. Completion is not cursor-paginated; the client narrows results by sending the updated partial value as the user types.

stem: What does a successful `prompts/get` result contain?

options.text: An optional `description` plus a `messages` array of `user` and `assistant` messages
options.why: Correct: the client can add these messages straight to the conversation.

options.text: A template string with `{placeholders}` that the client fills in with the user's argument values before sending
options.why: The server fills the arguments in and returns finished messages.

options.text: A single `system` message to prepend to the model's instructions
options.why: Prompt messages have only `user` and `assistant` roles; MCP has no system role here.

options.text: A list of tool calls the client should execute in order
options.why: Prompts return messages, not tool invocations.

explanation: `prompts/get` returns `messages`, each with a `role` (`user` or `assistant`) and one content block: text, image, audio, a resource link or an embedded resource. Arguments are substituted on the server, which is why servers SHOULD validate them.

stem: A client may treat a `nextCursor` whose value is the empty string `""` as the end of the results.

options.text: True
options.why: An empty string is a valid cursor; only a missing `nextCursor` signals the end.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: cursors are opaque, and the spec says an empty string is a valid cursor that MUST NOT be treated as the end of results.

explanation: Clients MUST treat cursors as opaque: no parsing, no modifying, and no decisions based on the value other than whether one was provided. An empty string counts as provided. Treat a missing `nextCursor` as the end, and expect `-32602` for an invalid cursor.

stem: A `resources/read` result contains the signed-in user's own notes. Which `cacheScope` should the server set?

options.text: `"private"`, so caches reuse it only within the same authorization context
options.why: Correct: user-specific data must not be shared across tokens.

options.text: `"user"`, matching the annotation audience
options.why: `cacheScope` has only two values, `public` and `private`.

options.text: Omit `cacheScope`, because `ttlMs` alone controls caching
options.why: `resources/read` results MUST carry both `ttlMs` and `cacheScope`.

options.text: `"public"`, because the request was authenticated and so only this user can ever receive it
options.why: Authentication does not stop sharing: a public response may be reused for other callers.

explanation: `cacheScope: "public"` means any client, gateway or proxy may serve the response to anyone. `"private"` limits reuse to the same authorization context, and caches MUST NOT be shared across contexts. Use `private` for per-user reads and for list results filtered per user.

stem: A client wants a file from a server that exposes only the template `file:///{path}`. Put the steps in order.

options.text: Use `completion/complete` to suggest values while the user types the `path` argument
Expand the template with the chosen value into a concrete URI
Call `resources/read` with that URI
Call `resources/templates/list` and find the template

explanation: Templates are discovered with `resources/templates/list`. Arguments can be auto-completed with `completion/complete` using a `ref/resource` reference to the template. The client expands the RFC 6570 template into a URI and reads it with `resources/read`.

stem: Which statements about resource annotations are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `priority` is an integer from 1 to 10
options.why: It is a number between 0.0 and 1.0.

options.text: `audience` may include `"system"` for content meant only for the system prompt
options.why: Only `user` and `assistant` are valid roles.

options.text: Annotations are enforced access controls that stop the model from seeing content
options.why: They are hints that help clients filter and prioritise; access control lives on the server.

options.text: `priority` ranges from 0.0 to 1.0, where 1 means the content is effectively required
options.why: Correct: 0 means entirely optional and 1 means most important.

options.text: `lastModified` is an ISO 8601 timestamp
options.why: Correct: for example `2025-01-12T15:00:58Z`.

explanation: Annotations (`audience`, `priority`, `lastModified`) appear on resources, resource templates and content blocks, including tool results and prompt messages. They help clients decide what to show, what to include in context and how to sort, but they enforce nothing.

stem: A client calls `prompts/get` for `code_review` but leaves out the argument `code`, which the prompt marks as `required: true`. What should the server return?

options.text: A JSON-RPC error with code `-32602` (Invalid params)
options.why: Correct: the spec lists missing required arguments as an Invalid params error.

options.text: A result whose message contains the literal text `{code}`
options.why: Returning a broken prompt hides the mistake from the user.

options.text: A JSON-RPC error with code `-32601` (Method not found)
options.why: The method exists; the arguments are what is wrong.

options.text: A result with `isError: true`
options.why: `isError` belongs to tool results; prompts report failures as JSON-RPC errors.

explanation: Prompt errors use standard JSON-RPC codes: `-32602` for an invalid prompt name or missing required arguments, `-32603` for internal errors. Servers SHOULD validate prompt arguments before processing them, and MUST validate prompt inputs and outputs to prevent injection.

stem: A user is filling in the `owner` argument of the template `github://repos/{owner}/{repo}`. Which `ref` should the client send in `completion/complete`?

options.text: `{"type": "ref/prompt", "name": "github://repos/{owner}/{repo}"}`
options.why: `ref/prompt` references a prompt by name, not a URI template.

options.text: `{"type": "ref/tool", "name": "github"}`
options.why: Completion covers prompt and resource-template arguments, not tool arguments.

options.text: `{"type": "ref/resource", "uri": "github://repos/{owner}/{repo}"}`
options.why: Correct: `ref/resource` takes a URI or URI template in `uri`.

options.text: `{"type": "ref/template", "template": "github://repos/{owner}/{repo}"}`
options.why: There is no `ref/template` type; templates are referenced through `ref/resource`.

explanation: `completion/complete` supports two reference types: `ref/prompt` (by prompt `name`) and `ref/resource` (by `uri`, which may be a URI template). The request also carries `argument` (`name` and current `value`) and optionally `context.arguments` with values already chosen.

stem: For the template `github://repos/{owner}/{repo}`, the user already chose `owner = modelcontextprotocol` and is now typing `repo = py`. How should the client get relevant suggestions?

options.text: Send `argument: {name: "repo", value: "modelcontextprotocol/py"}` so the server can split it
options.why: Values are per argument; packing two into one breaks the server's matching.

options.text: Call `resources/list` and filter repositories on the client
options.why: That bypasses completion and may list far more than the client needs.

options.text: Send `argument: {name: "repo", value: "py"}` and `context.arguments: {owner: "modelcontextprotocol"}`
options.why: Correct: earlier choices go in `context.arguments` so the server can narrow suggestions.

options.text: Nothing extra: the server remembers the `owner` value from the previous `completion/complete` request in this conversation
options.why: There is no session state; each request must carry its own context.

explanation: For prompts or templates with several arguments, clients should include previously resolved values in `context.arguments`. Servers SHOULD rank by relevance and may use fuzzy matching; clients SHOULD debounce rapid requests and may cache results.

stem: A tool generates a 40 MB log export. How should it hand the export back?

options.text: Embed the whole export as a `resource` content block so everything arrives in one response and nothing needs a second fetch
options.why: Inlining 40 MB swamps the result and the model's context for data that may never be needed.

options.text: Return a short summary plus a `resource_link` to the export, which the client can read if and when it needs to
options.why: Correct: a link keeps the result small and leaves fetching to the client.

options.text: Split the export across many `text` blocks in the same result
options.why: Splitting does not change the size of the response.

options.text: Return only the export's `https://` URL as plain text
options.why: If the client cannot fetch it directly, an `https` URI is the wrong scheme, and plain text loses the structured link.

explanation: Embed a resource when the content is small and needed right away; return a `resource_link` when the content is large, optional or reusable, so the client decides whether to read it. Linked resources do not have to appear in `resources/list`.

stem: A server holds profile data for millions of users. How should it expose profiles as resources?

options.text: Expose one resource whose contents hold every profile
options.why: Clients would download everything to use one record.

options.text: List every profile in `resources/list`, relying on cursor pagination to keep each individual page small
options.why: Millions of entries are expensive to list and useless to browse.

options.text: Publish a resource template such as `users://{id}/profile`, ideally with completion for `id`
options.why: Correct: templates expose parameterised resources without enumerating them.

options.text: Make a prompt that takes a user ID
options.why: Prompts are user-chosen message templates, not a way to address data.

explanation: Resource templates (RFC 6570 URI templates, listed by `resources/templates/list`) describe whole families of resources. They carry a name, title, description and MIME type, and their arguments can be auto-completed. Use direct resources for a small, fixed set.

stem: Under RFC 6570, what does the URI template `file:///{path}` expand to when `path` is `src/main.rs`?

options.text: Expansion fails because `/` is not allowed in a variable value
options.why: Any string is allowed; reserved characters are percent-encoded rather than rejected.

options.text: `file:///src/main.rs`
options.why: That is what reserved expansion, `{+path}`, produces; simple expansion encodes the slash.

options.text: `file:///src%2Fmain.rs`
options.why: Correct: simple `{var}` expansion percent-encodes reserved characters such as `/`.

options.text: `file:///{src/main.rs}`
options.why: Expansion replaces the whole expression, braces included.

explanation: Simple string expansion (`{var}`) percent-encodes everything outside the unreserved set, so `/` becomes `%2F`. Reserved expansion (`{+var}`) keeps reserved characters such as `/`. For multi-segment paths, `{+path}` is usually what you want, and matching code must agree on which form the template uses.

stem: An agent keeps acting on an old version of `file:///project/config.json` after the file changes. The server declares `"resources": {"subscribe": true}`. What is the 2026-07-28 fix?

options.text: Listen via `subscriptions/listen` (`resourceSubscriptions`) and re-read on each update notification
options.why: Correct: that is the 2026-07-28 subscription mechanism for per-resource updates.

options.text: Rely on `notifications/resources/list_changed`
options.why: That signals changes to which resources exist, not changes to a resource's content.

options.text: Call `resources/subscribe` with the URI and wait for updates
options.why: `resources/subscribe` and `resources/unsubscribe` were replaced in 2026-07-28.

options.text: Start a background job that re-reads the file every `ttlMs` milliseconds, so the copy is never older than one TTL
options.why: Clients SHOULD NOT treat the TTL as a polling interval, and polling still leaves a staleness window.

explanation: In 2025-11-25 a client called `resources/subscribe`. In 2026-07-28 it opens one `subscriptions/listen` stream and lists URIs in `resourceSubscriptions`; the server acknowledges and sends `notifications/resources/updated` with the URI, and the client re-reads it. `listChanged` covers additions and removals only.

stem: Which statements about MCP cache keys are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `input_required` interim results carry `ttlMs` and may be cached briefly
options.why: Interim results are not cacheable and carry no caching hints.

options.text: A cached `resources/read` for one URI can serve another URI on the same server
options.why: Different parameters mean a different cache entry.

options.text: Results of retried requests carrying `inputResponses` or `requestState` MUST NOT be cached
options.why: Correct: they depend on inputs that are not part of the cache key.

options.text: A client MUST NOT serve a cached response for a request whose method or parameters differ from the original
options.why: Correct: the key is the method plus the parameters that affect the result, such as `uri` or `cursor`.

options.text: Each page of a paginated list shares a single TTL that starts at the first page
options.why: Every page is cached independently, and its clock starts when that page arrives.

explanation: The cache key is the request method plus the parameters that affect the result. Multi round-trip retries are never cached, `input_required` results carry no hints, and paginated pages are cached independently with their own `ttlMs`.

stem: Which statements about `ttlMs` are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: A client MAY serve a stale cached response if re-fetching fails, for example during an outage
options.why: Correct: the spec allows serving stale data on errors.

options.text: Clients SHOULD refetch in the background every `ttlMs` milliseconds
options.why: Clients SHOULD NOT treat the TTL as a polling interval; any polling MUST use jitter and backoff.

options.text: A `ttlMs` of 0 means the response should be treated as immediately stale
options.why: Correct: the client may re-fetch every time it needs the data.

options.text: A negative `ttlMs` means the result may be cached forever
options.why: Clients SHOULD ignore negative values and treat them as 0, and servers MUST send values of 0 or more.

options.text: A TTL guarantees that the data will not change before it expires
options.why: It is a freshness hint; servers may change data before the TTL ends.

explanation: `ttlMs` works like HTTP `max-age`: fresh while `now < t_received + ttlMs`. Zero, absent or negative values mean immediately stale. The client checks freshness when it needs the data and re-fetches only if stale. It MAY re-fetch early if it suspects a change and MAY serve stale data when a re-fetch fails.

stem: If a list result has no `ttlMs`, clients should cache it indefinitely until a `list_changed` notification arrives.

options.text: True
options.why: The default for a missing `ttlMs` is 0, so the result is immediately stale.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: clients SHOULD assume 0 when `ttlMs` is absent and rely on their own heuristics or notifications. Only older servers should omit it.

explanation: Servers implementing 2026-07-28 MUST include `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` on `server/discover`, `tools/list`, `prompts/list`, `resources/list`, `resources/templates/list` and `resources/read` results. A missing TTL, which should only come from older servers, means immediately stale.

stem: A client cached `prompts/list` with `ttlMs: 600000`. Two minutes later a `notifications/prompts/list_changed` arrives. What should the client do?

options.text: Treat the cached list as stale now and re-fetch `prompts/list` when it next needs it
options.why: Correct: notifications act as an immediate invalidation signal on top of the TTL.

options.text: Apply the changes carried in the notification to the cached list
options.why: List-changed notifications carry no list; the client has to re-fetch.

options.text: Ignore it, because notifications only matter when the server sends no `ttlMs`
options.why: TTL and notifications are complementary; both can be used together.

options.text: Keep the cache until the 10 minutes run out, then re-fetch
options.why: A relevant notification invalidates a cached response even while it is fresh.

explanation: Servers may provide `ttlMs` with or without `listChanged`. When both are present, the TTL avoids unnecessary re-fetches between notifications, and a notification immediately invalidates the cached response. `notifications/prompts/list_changed` reaches clients listening with `promptsListChanged: true`.

stem: A server reads pages from an internal wiki over HTTPS using its own service credentials and exposes them as resources. Which URI scheme should it use?

options.text: No URI; return the page text from a tool instead
options.why: Resources need URIs, and the data is a good fit for a resource.

options.text: `file://`, because the pages behave like documents
options.why: `file://` is for filesystem-like resources, and it still misleads clients about how to fetch.

options.text: A custom scheme such as `wiki://`, so clients read it through the server
options.why: Correct: the client cannot fetch the page without the server's credentials, so a non-`https` scheme fits.

options.text: `https://`, because the content really does come from an HTTPS URL and clients should see the true origin
options.why: The spec says to use `https://` only when the client can fetch the resource directly itself.

explanation: Servers SHOULD use `https://` only when the client can load the resource from the web on its own. Otherwise they SHOULD use another scheme, or define a custom one that follows RFC 3986, even if the server itself downloads the content over the internet.

stem: You are designing an MCP server over a company knowledge base of 50,000 documents. Which two choices fit MCP's primitives best? (Choose two.)

options.text: Each document addressable as a resource through a template like `kb://docs/{id}`, with search hits returned as `resource_link` blocks
options.why: Correct: documents become readable context, and search results stay small.

options.text: All 50,000 documents listed in a single unpaginated `resources/list` response
options.why: Huge, slow and useless for selection; templates and search scale better.

options.text: A `search_documents(query)` tool that the model can call when it needs information
options.why: Correct: searching is a model-driven action with parameters, which is what tools are for.

options.text: The full text of every search hit embedded in the search result
options.why: Embedding everything floods context; links let the client read only what it needs.

options.text: Search as a prompt that the model invokes on its own
options.why: Prompts are user-controlled templates, not model-invoked actions.

explanation: A common retrieval design: a search tool the model calls, documents as resources (fixed or templated URIs) that the host or user can attach, and search results returned as resource links. Prompts can add user-chosen workflows such as "summarise this document".

stem: A user runs a server's `/code_review` prompt from the host's slash menu. Order what happens.

options.text: The host adds the returned messages to the conversation and sends them to the model
The host shows prompts from `prompts/list` and the user picks `code_review`
The host calls `completion/complete` to suggest values as the user types the `language` argument
The host sends `prompts/get` with the chosen arguments

explanation: Prompts are user-controlled: they are discovered with `prompts/list`, surfaced in UI such as slash commands, completed argument by argument with `completion/complete` (`ref/prompt`), resolved with `prompts/get`, and only then handed to the model as messages.

stem: Match each failure with the JSON-RPC error code the spec gives for it.

options.why: Invalid params.
Internal error.
Method not found.
Resource not found in earlier protocol versions.

prompts.text: `resources/read` for a URI that does not exist, on a 2026-07-28 server
The server's database crashes while reading a resource
`completion/complete` sent to a server that does not support completions
Resource not found, reported by a server on an older protocol version

explanation: In 2026-07-28 resource-not-found is `-32602`; clients SHOULD also accept `-32002` from older servers. Internal failures are `-32603`. The completion spec lists `-32601` for a server without the capability. Invalid prompt names, missing required arguments and invalid cursors are also `-32602`.

stem: A client calls `resources/read` on `file:///project/src/`, which the server describes with MIME type `inode/directory`. The result's `contents` array holds three entries, one per file. Is that valid?

options.text: Yes: servers MAY return multiple contents from one read, for example the files in a directory
options.why: Correct: each entry carries its own `uri`.

options.text: No: a read must return exactly one content item for the requested URI
options.why: The spec explicitly allows several contents in one read.

options.text: No: directories cannot be resources, because they have no standard MIME type
options.why: Servers MAY use XDG MIME types such as `inode/directory` for non-regular files.

options.text: Only if the server first lists each file in `resources/list`
options.why: There is no such requirement for the contents of a read.

explanation: A `resources/read` result may contain several content items, each with its own `uri`, `mimeType` and `text` or `blob`. For `file://` resources servers MAY use XDG MIME types like `inode/directory` for things such as directories, and `file://` resources need not map to a real filesystem.

stem: A client is deciding what to do with resources a server returned. Match each need with the field that serves it.

options.text: `audience`
options.why: Who the content is intended for: user, assistant or both.

options.text: `priority`
options.why: How important the content is, from 0.0 to 1.0.

options.text: `lastModified`
options.why: When the content last changed, as an ISO 8601 timestamp.

options.text: `mimeType`
options.why: The media type, which tells the client how to interpret and render the bytes.

prompts.text: Show an image to the human but leave it out of the model's context
Decide which attachments to keep when the context budget is tight
Sort attachments so the most recently changed come first
Decide whether to render the content as Markdown or as a PNG

explanation: `audience`, `priority` and `lastModified` are annotations, hints for filtering, prioritising and sorting. `mimeType` is a field on the resource and its contents that says what the data is.

stem: A client cached pages 1 and 2 of `resources/list`. Page 2 expires, and re-fetching it with its cursor returns `-32602` (invalid cursor). What should the client do?

options.text: Keep page 1 and request page 2 again without a cursor
options.why: A request without a cursor returns the first page, not page 2.

options.text: Discard every cached page and re-fetch the list from the beginning
options.why: Correct: an invalidated cursor means the cached pages can no longer be trusted together.

options.text: Retry the same cursor with backoff until the server accepts it
options.why: An invalid cursor will not become valid by retrying.

options.text: Rewrite the cursor value to point one page further back and try again
options.why: Cursors are opaque; clients MUST NOT parse or modify them.

explanation: Each page is cached independently with its own TTL and re-fetched with its cursor when stale. If a previously valid cursor becomes invalid, the client SHOULD discard all cached pages and start again without a cursor. Servers SHOULD provide stable cursors and SHOULD answer invalid ones with `-32602`.

stem: A `file://` resource server receives `resources/read` for `file:///srv/docs/..%2F..%2Fetc/passwd`. Which two measures does the spec require or most directly call for? (Choose two.)

options.text: Return an empty `contents` array so the attacker learns nothing
options.why: Servers MUST NOT use an empty array to mean not found; return an error.

options.text: Trust the client, because it only sends URIs that appeared in `resources/list`
options.why: Clients can send any URI, and templates make unlisted URIs normal.

options.text: Block requests whose raw URI contains the literal string `..`
options.why: Encoded forms such as `%2E%2E` or `..%2F` slip past a literal check.

options.text: Validate every resource URI the server receives
options.why: Correct: servers MUST validate all resource URIs.

options.text: Decode and canonicalise the path, then refuse anything that resolves outside the allowed root
options.why: Correct: servers MUST sanitise file paths to prevent directory traversal.

explanation: Resource security considerations: servers MUST validate all resource URIs, SHOULD apply access controls and check permissions, MUST encode binary data properly, and MUST sanitise file paths to prevent directory traversal for `file://` resources. Canonicalise first, then check the result against the allowed root.

stem: You are designing an MCP file-reading assistant over a monorepo with two million files. Which design fits MCP best?

options.text: One `read_any_file(path)` tool and no resources at all, returning each whole file inline as a text block
options.why: It removes the application's ability to attach files and returns unbounded content into context.

options.text: List all two million files in `resources/list` so the user can browse them
options.why: Enumerating everything is slow, and the host cannot present it usefully.

options.text: A `repo://files/{+path}` template with completion, plus a `search_code` tool returning `resource_link`s
options.why: Correct: it addresses files without enumerating them, lets the model search, and keeps reads small and safely cached.

options.text: A prompt per directory that embeds every file in that directory
options.why: Prompts are user-chosen templates; embedding whole directories floods the conversation.

explanation: Large corpora call for templates (with completion) rather than enumeration, a search tool for model-driven discovery that returns links rather than content, sensible caching scopes, and path validation on the server. `{+path}` keeps slashes in multi-segment paths.

stem: A server filters `tools/list` by each caller's OAuth scopes but marks every result `cacheScope: "public"`. Behind a shared caching gateway, what goes wrong, and what is the fix?

options.text: The gateway will reject the response, because authenticated results cannot be public
options.why: Public responses from authenticated endpoints are allowed; that is exactly the risk.

options.text: Nothing: `cacheScope` is advisory and gateways cache only `resources/read`
options.why: Gateways MAY cache any public response, including list results.

options.text: Users get stale lists after scope changes; lower `ttlMs` to 0 so every request reaches the server
options.why: Staleness is not the issue; the leak is cross-user sharing, which `ttlMs: 0` does not fix reliably.

options.text: Users may get each other's filtered lists; mark them `private` and keep per-call access checks
options.why: Correct: public responses can cross authorization contexts, and the spec says not to rely on `cacheScope` alone for access control.

explanation: A `public` response may be stored and served to any user, even if it came from an authenticated call. Lists that vary per user should be `private`. Servers MUST still apply per-primitive access controls and MUST NOT rely on `cacheScope` to prevent unauthorized access.

stem: You build a multi-tenant MCP gateway that caches `resources/read` results keyed by method and `uri`. Users report seeing other people's documents. Results are correctly marked `private`. What is the bug?

options.text: The gateway should not cache `resources/read` at all
options.why: Reads are cacheable; private ones just need the right key.

options.text: Private responses were shared across authorization contexts; the cache key must also include the caller's authorization context
options.why: Correct: caches of private responses MUST NOT be shared across authorization contexts.

options.text: The client should have sent a `cacheScope` in the request
options.why: `cacheScope` is a field on results, set by the server.

options.text: The server should have set a shorter `ttlMs`
options.why: A shorter TTL narrows the window but still leaks between users.

explanation: `private` means the response may be reused only within the same authorization context, so a different access token needs a different cache. The method-plus-parameters key is necessary but not sufficient for private data.

stem: A client treats `contents.length === 0` from `resources/read` as "resource not found". It talks to both 2026-07-28 servers and older ones. What should it do instead?

options.text: Treat only `-32002` as not found, since that is the resource-specific code
options.why: That was the old code; 2026-07-28 servers send `-32602`.

options.text: Treat `-32602` (and `-32002` from older servers) as not found, and an empty `contents` array as an existing but empty resource
options.why: Correct: this follows the current rule and the backwards-compatibility advice.

options.text: Treat any JSON-RPC error from `resources/read` as not found
options.why: Internal errors (`-32603`) and others would be misreported as missing.

options.text: Keep the check; servers return empty contents for missing resources
options.why: 2026-07-28 servers MUST NOT return an empty array for a missing resource.

explanation: The 2026-07-28 rules: not found is `-32602` (often with `data.uri`), internal errors are `-32603`, and an empty `contents` array never means not found, because it would be ambiguous. Clients SHOULD also accept `-32002` from servers on earlier versions.

stem: A server offers a `summarize_ticket(ticket_id)` prompt whose message embeds the customer-written ticket text. Which two measures follow from the prompts spec's security requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Return the ticket text in a `system` role message so it carries more weight
options.why: Prompt messages have only `user` and `assistant` roles, and elevating untrusted text is the wrong direction.

options.text: Skip checks, because prompts are user-controlled and therefore trusted
options.why: User-controlled is about who triggers the prompt, not about trusting its inputs or embedded content.

options.text: Let the model call `prompts/get` itself whenever it sees a ticket number
options.why: That turns a user-controlled prompt into a model-controlled one; tools exist for that.

options.text: Validate `ticket_id` before using it
options.why: Correct: servers SHOULD validate prompt arguments, and implementations MUST validate prompt inputs.

options.text: Check that the requesting caller may access that ticket before embedding it
options.why: Correct: the spec calls for validation that prevents unauthorized access to resources.

explanation: Implementations MUST carefully validate all prompt inputs and outputs to prevent injection attacks or unauthorized access to resources. A prompt that pulls in third-party text can carry prompt-injection payloads, and an unchecked argument can expose data the user should not see.

stem: A `customer_email` prompt argument offers completion. Any signed-in user typing `a` sees emails of all customers. Which two measures does the completion spec call for? (Choose two.)

options.text: Nothing, because the 100-value cap already limits exposure
options.why: Repeated prefixes enumerate everything 100 values at a time.

options.text: Set `hasMore: false` so users cannot tell more emails exist
options.why: Hiding the count does not stop disclosure of the values themselves.

options.text: Move completion to the client by sending it the full email list once
options.why: That discloses everything at once.

options.text: Rate limit completion requests
options.why: Correct: rate limiting is a MUST in the security section, and it slows enumeration through repeated prefixes.

options.text: Control access to sensitive suggestions, returning only values the caller may see
options.why: Correct: implementations MUST control access to sensitive suggestions and prevent completion-based information disclosure.

explanation: Completion security: implementations MUST validate inputs, rate limit, control access to sensitive suggestions and prevent completion-based information disclosure. Treat completion as a data endpoint with the same authorization as the underlying data.

stem: An assistant needs live currency exchange rates mid-reasoning, whenever a user's question involves converting money. Should the server expose them as a resource or a tool?

options.text: A read-only tool such as `get_exchange_rate(from, to)`, optionally also a resource for apps that want to attach it
options.why: Correct: when the model must decide when to fetch, it needs a model-controlled primitive.

options.text: A prompt that embeds today's rates
options.why: Prompts are user-triggered; the user would have to invoke it every time.

options.text: A resource with `priority: 1.0` so the host always includes it
options.why: Priority is a hint, and always attaching live rates wastes context when they are not needed.

options.text: A resource only, because the data is read-only
options.why: Read-only does not settle it: resources are application-driven, so the model cannot count on fetching one mid-reasoning.

explanation: Choosing between resource and tool depends on control, not just side effects. If the model must decide when to fetch data, a read-only tool is the reliable choice; resources suit context the host or user selects. Exposing both is fine when both uses exist.

stem: A server marks `tools/list` with `ttlMs: 300000` and supports `listChanged`. Put these client events in order.

options.text: The client fetches `tools/list` and caches it for five minutes
`notifications/tools/list_changed` arrives and the client marks the cache stale
The next time the list is needed, the client calls `tools/list` again
Two minutes later the client needs the list again and uses the cached copy

explanation: The TTL avoids re-fetching while the response is fresh; a list-changed notification immediately invalidates it, and the client re-fetches on next access rather than on a timer.

stem: A client pages through `resources/list` over ten minutes while documents are being added, and ends up with one resource twice. What is the right explanation and fix?

options.text: The server should have used `hasMore` instead of `nextCursor`
options.why: `hasMore` belongs to completion results.

options.text: The client used an expired cursor; it should parse the cursor to find the right position
options.why: Cursors are opaque and must not be parsed.

options.text: Pages are independent, so changes between fetches can cause duplicates or gaps; for a consistent snapshot, re-fetch from the beginning
options.why: Correct: that is the spec's guidance.

options.text: The server is buggy: cursors guarantee a consistent snapshot
options.why: There is no cross-page consistency guarantee.

explanation: Each page is fetched and cached independently. If the data changes between page fetches, duplicates and gaps are possible. Clients that need a consistent view SHOULD re-fetch the whole list from the start without a cursor, and can also de-duplicate by URI.

stem: A team wants a "generate release notes for version X" workflow that pulls the git log and changelog as context. A user always starts it deliberately. Which design fits best?

options.text: A system prompt shipped by the server that tells the model to write notes when asked
options.why: Servers have no system-prompt primitive; prompts return user and assistant messages.

options.text: A prompt with a `version` argument (with completion), whose messages embed or link the git log and changelog resources
options.why: Correct: a user-initiated, parameterised workflow is what prompts are for, and they can carry resources.

options.text: A tool `generate_release_notes` that the model calls when it thinks a release is near
options.why: This gives control to the model, but the user wants to start the workflow deliberately.

options.text: A resource `releases://{version}/notes` the host attaches automatically to every chat
options.why: Attaching it everywhere wastes context, and a resource does not express a user-triggered workflow.

explanation: Prompts are user-controlled, accept arguments (which can be completed) and return messages that may include embedded resources or resource links. That makes them a natural fit for repeatable, user-triggered workflows that need server context.
